sentences.text: Thecachampsa possessed a long, slender snout similar to that of living gharials, and its teeth were long and recurved.
Unlike its living relatives, Thecachampsa was a marine animal that inhabited estuaries and shallow coastal waters.

American paleontologist Joseph Leidy described the species Crocodylus antiquus in 1852 from Miocene deposits in Virginia, using a tooth found in the Calvert Formation as the holotype — the specimen the species is based on.

Edward Drinker Cope erected the genus Thecachampsa in 1867, originally containing two species based on teeth without a designated type species, before designating T. sericodon as the type species in 1882.
Cope named the species T. sicaria in 1869 based on a jaw fragment and a dorsal vertebra, noting that its teeth were lenticular in cross-section with sharp cutting edges.
He also named T. fastigiata in 1870 as a reassignment of a species originally named by Leidy in 1852, as species within Thecachampsa were primarily distinguished by differences in tooth shape.
The genus was synonymized with Crocodylus in 1973 but is now considered valid, and in 2001, A.C. Myrick synonymized Gavialosuchus americanus with T. antiqua.
A younger species was first described as Tomistoma americanus in 1915 from Florida, with remains found in formations across New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia, and North Carolina.
There are 39 recorded fossil occurrences of Thecachampsa in the Paleobiology Database.
Thecachampsa belongs to the parent group Gavialoidea and is classified within the class Reptilia.
Fossils of Thecachampsa range in age from the late Early Miocene to the early Pliocene, and remains have been found in Florida, California, Baja California, and Costa Rica.
It is debated whether different tooth shapes represent distinct species or variations within a single species, as complete skulls showing these variations were previously referred to Gavialosuchus.
